issues.failure_explanation: The proof of (i) says the right-hand side of the ODE for w~ is continuous, hence locally Lipschitz, and then invokes uniqueness. Continuity does not give Lipschitz continuity; A2 only asks sigma_rp to be C^1. For sigma_rp(z)=|z|^{2/p}, the field has the factor sigma'(w)^2 = (4/p^2) w~^{2-p}, which is non-Lipschitz at 0 for p in (1,2). The 'constant trajectory' argument is also not legitimate for a coupled system. The conclusion itself fails. Take p=3/2, N=2, A=[1,1], y=1, squared loss, w~_0=(4,eps^2). Then sqrt(w~_2) decreases at rate (8/9)r with r the residual, and the total decrease exceeds eps for small eps. So w~_2 reaches 0 in finite time, and w~(t) leaves int(D_rp^N), contradicting (i).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a local Lipschitz condition on sigma_rp' (or on sigma_rp'^2 as a function of w~) to A2. This restricts the polynomial results to p<=1 (and p=1), or requires a separate argument for p in (1,2), where the interior property is false in general.
issues.overall_effect: Part (i) and everything that uses the interior property are unreliable for general A2-reparametrizations. This covers the polynomial results for p in (1,2), which the introduction advertises for all p in (0,2). The interior property enters Lemma lem:decay and Theorem thm:Convergence.
issues.title: Invariance of the interior (Thm. part (i)) proved by 'continuous implies locally Lipschitz'; false for non-Lipschitz reparametrizations such as p in (1,2)
issues.why_classification: The central trajectory-control claim is false as stated. Any valid version excludes part of the advertised regime p in (1,2) or needs new arguments.

issues.failure_explanation: Item (ii) claims that f=g(A·) inherits the PL constant sigma_min^2 mu whenever g is PL with mu. This is false. Take g(v)=(v_1-v_2)^2/2, which is PL with mu=2 since |∇g|^2=4g. Take A=e_1, so sigma_min=1. Then f(z)=z^2/2 has |f'|^2=2f, i.e. PL constant only 1, not 2. The gradient A^T∇g(Av) need not carry the full norm of the range(A) component of ∇g. The argument needs strong convexity, or convexity plus quadratic growth with a worse constant. The step in the proof of Theorem thm:Convergence (ii) that uses the remark inherits this error.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the remark for strongly convex g. Alternatively, with L(·,y) convex and PL, derive PL with constant mu/4 times sigma_min^2 from quadratic growth plus convexity, and adjust the rate constant. The linear rate survives.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit rate exp(-2 r mu sigma_min^2 t) in Thm. thm:Convergence (ii), and the linear-rate claims in the corollaries, are not justified with the stated constants.
issues.title: Remark on Polyak-Lojasiewicz constant under composition with A is false for general PL functions
issues.why_classification: A short contained lemma and a changed constant fix it, and the qualitative linear-rate conclusion survives.

issues.failure_explanation: Part (ii) needs a uniform lower bound r on the entries of h'^{-1}(w~(t)), i.e. a lower bound on w~(t) away from 0. The proof defers this to the reader as a 'refinement'. The only available mechanism is the monotone bound on D_F(z~_0, w~(t)) from Lemma lem:decay. That bound depends on the interior solution z~_0, i.e. on y, so the claimed dependence of c on only p, mu, w~_0, A is inaccurate. The same gap occurs for the tanh case in Cor. cor:TrigonometricRegularizationConvergence (ii), where r' is again deferred.

issues.failure_explanation: When h or H blow up at the boundary, the proof restricts to a smaller domain D_circ. It asserts that for every z~_circ in D_circ^N and every z~ outside D_circ^N the objective at z~_circ is at most that at z~. This cannot hold for all pairs: a z~_circ far from the minimizer can have a larger value than an outside z~ near the minimizer. No domain is constructed and no proof is given. The extension from the shrunk domain to the whole feasible set needs a separate argument, for instance convexity together with the fact that w~_inf is interior to D_circ^N, so a minimizer over D_circ^N is a local and hence global minimizer.

issues.failure_explanation: Lemma lem:decay and Theorem thm:Convergence (i), (iii) are stated under A3, which only requires L to be C^1 with a unique zero. The proof uses convexity of L(·,y), and it uses L~(z~_0)=0, i.e. A z~_0 = y, even though the lemma says 'for any z~_0 in int'. Convexity fails in general. Example: N=M=1, A=1, sigma_rp=sinh, L(v,y)=(v-y)^2((v-y-2)^2+0.1). This L has a unique zero but a second strict local minimum near v-y≈1.95 with value ≈0.4. A flow started in that basin converges to a point with positive loss, contradicting 'lim A w~(t)=y' and the O(1/t) bound with D_F<infinity.

issues.failure_explanation: For p<=1 (and for tanh) the proof needs w~_inf to lie in the interior, because h and H diverge at the boundary. It gets this by applying Lemma lem:decay with a feasible z~ in the interior, using that D_F(z~,u_k) tends to infinity as a coordinate of u_k tends to the boundary. The corollary does not assume B2 (an interior z~_0 with A z~_0 = y), so such a z~ need not exist. If every nonnegative solution has a zero entry, then D_F(z~,u_k) stays finite as u_k tends to the boundary and the argument gives nothing. The theorem hypotheses (interior limit, or finite h and H) are then not verified. The same gap affects the tanh case and the asymptotic corollaries, whose statements also omit B2.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the B2 hypothesis (existence of an interior z~_0 with A z~_0 = y), and convexity from ISSUE-005, to cor:PolynomialRegularization, cor:PolynomialRegularizationNonAsymptotic and the tanh part of the trigonometric corollaries.
issues.overall_effect: The p<=1 and tanh variants of the implicit-bias corollaries are not proved at the stated generality. They hold only when an interior exact solution exists, as assumed in the introductory theorems but not in the corollaries.
issues.title: Non-asymptotic polynomial/tanh results argue the limit is interior via Lemma lem:decay without assuming an interior solution
issues.why_classification: The missing hypothesis is the standard one already assumed in the introductory theorems, so adding it preserves the results as advertised.
